title: The well of eighty-four steps
hookLine: at Goindval, Guru Amar Das builds a step-well open to every caste
tomorrow: first the row, then the audience

lines: THIRSTY, NEXT TO A FULL WELL.
GURU AMAR DAS BEGINS TO DIG.
cards: Imagine being thirsty next to a well full of clean water, and not being allowed to drink from it. Not because it's private property. Because of the family you were born into.
For centuries across South Asia, caste decided things like that: who could draw water from which well, who could eat with whom, who could touch whose cup.
The man who had carried water for twelve years in the dark was now the third Guru, Guru Amar Das. He settled at Goindval, on the banks of the river Beas. And there he began to dig.
Not a normal well. Something grander, and open to everyone.

teach.h: BAOLI — A WELL YOU WALK DOWN INTO.
teach.b: It's called a baoli: a step-well. Instead of lowering a bucket on a rope, you walk down a long staircase into the earth until you reach the water.

Step-wells are found across South Asia, some of them wonderfully beautiful. The one at Goindval has eighty-four steps, and it's still there today. What made it different: Guru Amar Das opened it to everyone.
Every caste, every family, walked down the same steps and drew from the same water. In a world where a shared well could be a scandal, that was a quiet revolution, built of brick and stone.
It also turned Goindval into a center for the Sikhs, a place people traveled to, and the first great Sikh place of pilgrimage. Now the number.
Eighty-four is significant in Indian thought: tradition spoke of eighty-four lakh, or eight point four million, forms of life a soul might pass through.
Sikh tradition says that a person who recites Guru Nanak's Japji on each of the eighty-four steps, bathing at each, can be freed from that long round of births.
Many pilgrims still do it, going down step by step.

Sikhs hold that practice in different ways: some as a promise, some as a devotional discipline, some as a picture of the long way down to the water of life. But everyone agrees on the baoli's first lesson.
The water at the bottom doesn't know anyone's caste. It's the same for all who walk down to it.

how: Pilgrims visit the Baoli Sahib at Goindval, where many walk down the eighty-four steps reciting the Japji and bathing; the well is remembered as a place Guru Amar Das opened to people of every caste.

games.q: you're building a well in a world where caste decides who may drink where. who gets to walk down the steps?
o: everyone, from every caste, to the same water.
games.why: Guru Amar Das opened the baoli at Goindval to all. the water at the bottom doesn't know anyone's caste.

practice: Pour a glass of water, hold it and look at it, then sip slowly, letting each sip sit before you swallow. Think of where it came from, a river, a reservoir, rain, and of someone, somewhere, who is thirsty right now.
If you pray, you can give thanks for water as you finish the glass.

wordCard.voice: Baoli. A step-well; the one at Goindval has eighty-four steps, and Guru Amar Das opened it to every caste. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: baoli, a step-well; Sikhs call the one at Goindval Baoli Sahib.
